newsitem.title: UK: U.S., UK could patrol no-fly zone without France.
newsitem.headline: U.S., UK could patrol no-fly zone without France.

text.p: The United States and Britain agreed on Thursday that they could patrol an extended no-fly zone over southern Iraq without France if Paris refuses to drop its objections to the operation against Saddam Hussein.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said after talks with British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind that he hoped France would come overcome its coolness towards two U.S. cruise missile attacks against Iraq this week.
But U.S. officials made clear that patrols could still be mounted over the extended no-fly zone whatever Paris decided.

"In discussions on the no-fly zone they agreed that no matter what the French do the U.S and the U.K. have the capability to implement effectively the no-fly zone," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"We've got sufficient air assets in the region to implement the extended no fly zone."
After his talks with Rifkind, Christopher flew immediately to Paris for talks with French President Jacques Chirac and Foreign Minister Herve de Charette.
"I hope that after our conversations this afternoon that the French will go forward with the operations as we have had in the past," Christopher said.
France was an important member of the U.S.-led coalition which drove Iraqi invasion forces out of Kuwait in 1991.

Britain has strongly supported the United States in its decision to extend the limit of the air exclusion zone in southern Iraq to the 33rd parallel, on the outskirts of Baghdad, from the 32nd parallel where it was fixed after the Gulf War.

France had a critical part in enforcing the initial, more limited no-fly zone. The United States fired a total of 44 cruise missiles on Iraq on Tuesday and Wednesday on air defence targets in southern Iraq to minimise Iraqi resistance to its warplanes policing the expanded no-fly zone.
"I think we have brought home to Saddam Hussein that there is a very high price for the kind of repressive conduct that he has taken in northern Iraq," Christopher said.
"This is Saddam playing his old reckless game -- one which the international community has to stand up to or we will find him feeling that he has a licence to go on.
"The only kind of language he understands is the language of force," Christopher said.
Rifkind said: "It is crucially necessary that whenever Saddam initiates repression or aggression that he should end up losing more than he thinks he has gained."
Christopher welcomed Britain's backing for the cruise missile attacks, instigated after the Iraqi leader moved forces into Kurdish areas of northern Iraq.
Christopher praised what he called the "extraordinary" partnership between Washington and London.
"We are very grateful to Prime Minister (John) Major, Foreign Secretary Rifkind and the entire British government for their unstinting support," he said.

Christopher said that despite criticism of the U.S. action against Iraq, he was confident that, as in the past when action had been taken against aggressors, other countries would overcome their objections and follow Washington's lead.

"We haven't always had support on the first day or the first week, but over time the world community has come to recognise and get behind those who show leadership to face up to the aggressors," he said.
After his talks in Paris, Christopher was due to go to Germany, where he will meet Chancellor Helmut Kohl and deliver a lecture on European security.
